epithet.en: King of Lydia, last of the Mermnadae, byword for wealth
epithet.da: Lydiernes konge, den sidste Mermnader, symbol på rigdom

6.modern-en: Herodotus introduces Croesus as the first barbarian known to have made contact with the Greeks — through conquest and through gifts to their sanctuaries. He is the son of Alyattes, ruler of all nations west of the Halys River, and the first to reduce Greek cities in Ionia to tributary status. His reign marks the moment when the Greek and non-Greek worlds are drawn into collision.

29.modern-en: Solon the Athenian visits Croesus at Sardis, the wealthiest court in the world. Croesus, proud of his treasure, shows it all off and asks Solon to name the happiest man he has ever seen — expecting to be named himself. Solon names an obscure Athenian, Tellus, who died fighting for his city and was honored with a public burial. The conversation plants the theme that will define Croesus's story.

30.modern-en: Solon continues by naming the Argive brothers Cleobis and Biton as the second happiest men he knows. When Croesus demands to know where he himself ranks, Solon tells him that no one can be called happy before they die — that all great prosperity is vulnerable to ruin at any moment. Croesus dismisses him as a fool, but the warning echoes through everything that follows.

46.modern-en: Worried by the rising power of Cyrus, Croesus tests the Greek oracles to find which speaks the truth. Only the oracle at Delphi correctly describes what he is doing at the exact moment of the test — boiling a tortoise and lamb together in a bronze cauldron. He showers Delphi with gifts and consults it about whether he should attack Persia.

53.modern-en: Delphi answers Croesus that if he attacks Persia he will destroy a great empire. He interprets this as a promise of victory, not realizing it could mean his own empire. He consults again about whether his dynasty will endure, and receives the response that it will last until a mule becomes king of the Medes — a riddle he takes as a guarantee of permanence.

72.modern-en: Croesus marches into Cappadocia to make war on Cyrus, motivated by both territorial ambition and a desire for revenge on Cyrus for overthrowing his brother-in-law Astyages. After an inconclusive battle in Pteria, he disbands his army for the winter and sends for allied forces — not realizing that Cyrus will follow him immediately rather than wait.

78.modern-en: Cyrus pursues Croesus back to Sardis immediately after the battle, not giving him time to reassemble his forces. Croesus deploys his famous Lydian cavalry — the finest in the world — but Cyrus counters by placing camels at the front of his line; Lydian horses, terrified by the camels' smell, bolt and throw their riders. The battle is lost before it begins.

86.modern-en: Sardis falls and Croesus is captured. Cyrus orders him bound and placed atop a great pyre to be burned alive. At the last moment, Croesus recalls Solon's warning — that no one should be called happy before he dies — and cries out Solon's name three times. Cyrus, moved by curiosity and pity, orders the fire quenched, but it burns too fiercely for the soldiers to put out. Apollo sends rain at Croesus's prayer, and the fire dies.

87.modern-en: Cyrus, having saved Croesus, seats him beside himself as an honored counselor. Croesus watches silently as Persians sack his city, then turns to Cyrus and asks: 'What are all those men doing?' When told they are plundering his city, he gently corrects him — 'They are plundering your city now' — and persuades Cyrus to take tribute instead, saving both the city and the Persian army from corruption.

89.modern-en: Cyrus, impressed by Croesus's counsel, treats him with great respect and keeps him close as an advisor. Croesus turns his captivity into a new kind of influence: the fallen king who understands fortune's reversal becomes the Persian court's most valuable voice of wisdom. His transformation from the world's richest king to wise counselor is one of Herodotus's great narrative pivots.

90.modern-en: Croesus sends back to Delphi to complain that the oracle misled him, and the Pythia responds that the oracle told the truth — if Croesus had asked what empire would be destroyed, he would have been told his own. She adds that Croesus's fall is the delayed punishment for his ancestor Gyges's crime. Croesus accepts the oracle's logic and declares that the fault was his own in misreading it.

91.modern-en: Herodotus catalogs the immense gifts Croesus had given to Greek sanctuaries — golden tripods, silver bowls, statues of lions, and much more — physical monuments to the wealth that had made him the most famous king of his age. Even in ruin, the scale of his devotion to the gods is visible across every major sanctuary in Greece. The gifts outlast the kingdom.

epithet.en: Founder of the Persian Empire, conqueror of Lydia and Babylon
epithet.da: Grundlæggeren af det persiske rige, erobrer af Lydien og Babylon

107.modern-en: Astyages, king of the Medes, dreams that a vine grows from the womb of his daughter Mandane and overspreads all Asia — a dream his interpreters explain as prophecy that her child will rule in his place. To prevent this, he marries her to a Persian of low rank, and when she bears a son he orders the child killed. The man entrusted with the murder cannot bring himself to carry it out.

109.modern-en: The infant Cyrus is given to the herdsman Mitradates to expose on a hillside. By providential coincidence, Mitradates's own wife has just given birth to a stillborn child; the couple swap the infants, raise Cyrus as their own, and bury the dead child as if it were the king's order fulfilled. Cyrus grows up a herdsman's son, with no idea of his origin.

120.modern-en: When Cyrus is ten, his royal bearing in childhood games gives away his true identity. Astyages, advised by dream-interpreters that the prophecy has already been fulfilled in the harmless game-playing of a child, releases Cyrus to his true parents in Persia. The terrible prophecy appears to have been defused — but it has not.

125.modern-en: Cyrus, now a young man in Persia, acts on a letter from Harpagus and begins rallying the Persians against Median rule. He tricks them into clearing thorny land for a day, then leads them to a feast and asks which labor they prefer: the exhausting work or feasting as free men. When they choose freedom, he tells them that obedience to Astyages means the former, revolt the latter. The Persians rise.

128.modern-en: Cyrus defeats and captures Astyages, his own grandfather. Harpagus, who had originally been ordered to kill the infant Cyrus and had spared him, comes forward to mock the fallen Astyages — pointing out that his own act of mercy decades ago has now brought about the very overthrow the king had tried to prevent. Astyages is kept alive but dethroned; Cyrus becomes king of the Medes and Persians.

153.modern-en: After defeating Croesus and installing a Persian governor in Lydia, Cyrus departs east while the Lydians immediately revolt. He returns and crushes the rebellion, but spares Croesus's life again. On Croesus's advice, he disarms the Lydians entirely — turning a warrior nation into merchants and musicians — rather than killing them. It is Croesus's most consequential piece of counsel.

177.modern-en: Cyrus turns his attention to Babylon, the most heavily fortified city in the world, ringed by enormous walls and provisioned for years of siege. Rather than assault the walls directly, he diverts the Euphrates into a lake bed his engineers have prepared, lowering the river until his soldiers can wade through the channel into the city. Babylon falls in a single night, taken completely by surprise.

207.modern-en: Approaching war against the Massagetae and Queen Tomyris, Cyrus receives conflicting advice from his generals. Croesus — now serving as his counselor — urges a bold crossing into Massagetae territory. Cyrus accepts the plan and sends Croesus away from the campaign to spare him from the danger. The choice to press forward rather than wait will prove fatal.

211.modern-en: Queen Tomyris, after her son is taken prisoner by Cyrus's stratagem with wine, sends him a fierce message: do not be puffed up, for you conquered by wine, not by war. She demands the return of her son and threatens to give Cyrus all the blood he can drink. Cyrus ignores the warning. Her son dies in captivity and she prepares for total war.

214.modern-en: Cyrus leads the Persian army deep into Massagetae territory and is defeated in a great battle — the worst defeat the Persians had yet suffered. Cyrus himself is killed in the fighting. Tomyris cuts off his head, fills a wineskin with human blood, and plunges his head into it, fulfilling her promise that she would give him his fill of blood. The greatest conqueror of the age ends his story in ignominious defeat.

epithet.en: Persian king who conquered Egypt and descended into madness
epithet.da: Persisk konge der erobrede Ægypten og endte i vanvid

398.modern-en: Cambyses launches his campaign against Egypt, ostensibly because Amasis refused to give him a royal Egyptian bride and substituted a lesser woman in her place. He marches with a combined force of Persians, Ionians, and Aeolians. The true motivation — conquest — is evident; the bride story is the pretext. Amasis dies before Cambyses arrives, and it falls to his son Psammenitos to defend Egypt.

411.modern-en: Memphis falls and Cambyses humiliates the captured Egyptian king Psammenitos publicly — marching his daughter in slave's clothing and his son off to be executed before his eyes. The other Egyptians weep and lament, but Psammenitos sits silent and motionless until he sees one of his own elderly friends being led away to beg for his living. Only then does he cry. Cambyses, moved by this reaction, tries unsuccessfully to spare the son.

420.modern-en: Cambyses sends spies to Ethiopia disguised as traders bearing gifts. The Ethiopian king sees through the ruse immediately, examines the gifts with contempt, and returns a great unstrung bow to Cambyses with the message: when the Persians can draw this bow, then let them come to fight the Ethiopians — until then they should thank the gods for not inspiring the Ethiopians to desire foreign land. Cambyses is humiliated and immediately launches a chaotic campaign he has not properly prepared.

430.modern-en: Herodotus catalogs the acts of madness Cambyses committed: killing his own brother Smerdis out of jealousy, killing his sister-wife in a fit of rage, desecrating the tombs of Egyptian pharaohs and mocking their gods. He stabbed the Apis bull that the Egyptians worshipped as divine — an act the Egyptians attributed to madness. Herodotus suggests that Cambyses may have suffered from epilepsy from birth, or that the sacrilege against Apis drove him mad.

462.modern-en: Cambyses, dying from a sword wound to the thigh accidentally self-inflicted in the same place where he had stabbed the Apis bull, confesses to his Persian nobles that he had secretly killed his brother Smerdis — and that the man now reigning in Persia as Smerdis is an impostor Magian. He begs them to recover the empire for the true Persian royal line. His death leaves the throne to the usurper he has just exposed.

463.modern-en: Cambyses dies of the wound, having reigned seven years and five months, leaving no heirs. His final act is a confession that exposes the Magian usurpation he had set in motion by his paranoid killing of his brother. The empire he leaves behind is in the hands of a false king — and it will fall to Darius and six conspirators to set things right.

epithet.en: Persian Great King, organizer of empire, defeated at Marathon
epithet.da: Persisk Storkonge, rigets organisator, besejret ved Marathon

470.modern-en: Gobryas rallies six Persian nobles — including Darius — to act against the Magian impostor who has seized the throne. He argues that if they wait for a better moment, the Magian will find them out and they will die anyway; better to die trying. Darius, the boldest of the group, argues for immediate action rather than recruiting allies. The conspiracy of six becomes the founding act of the new Persian order.

477.modern-en: After killing the Magian impostor, the six conspirators debate the ideal form of government — democracy, oligarchy, or monarchy. Otanes argues for democracy; Megabyzus for oligarchy; Darius makes the strongest case for monarchy, arguing that one excellent ruler surpasses the competing factions of the other systems. The seven agree that whoever's horse neighs first at sunrise shall be king.

483.modern-en: Darius wins the kingship through a trick engineered by his groom: the horse is brought to a spot near a mare the night before, and at the agreed time it naturally neighs. The moment it does so, lightning and thunder break from a clear sky — as if heaven itself confirms the choice. Darius becomes Great King of Persia, son of Hystaspes, and the other six nobles receive lifelong privileges at court.

487.modern-en: Darius organizes the Persian Empire into twenty tribute-paying satrapies, assigning a fixed annual tribute to each. Herodotus details the amounts: India pays the most of any single satrapy, in gold dust; Egypt provides enormous grain surpluses. The systematic organization of the empire into a revenue-bearing machine is Darius's distinctive achievement — where Cyrus conquered, Darius administered.

980.modern-en: Darius, furious over the Athenian role in burning Sardis during the Ionian Revolt, is said to have had a servant remind him of the Athenians at every dinner by saying three times: 'Master, remember the Athenians.' He dismisses one general — his own son-in-law Mardonius — after a naval disaster in the north, and sends a new expedition under Datis and Artaphernes directly toward Athens and Eretria.

996.modern-en: The Persian fleet under Datis arrives at Marathon after sacking Eretria. The Athenians debate whether to fight or wait for Spartan reinforcements; the war-archon Callimachus breaks the deadlock in favor of battle. The general Miltiades, who knows Persian tactics from his years in the Chersonese, proposes thinning the center and strengthening the wings — a formation that will prove decisive.

999.modern-en: The Battle of Marathon is fought. The Athenians charge the Persians at a run across nearly a mile of open ground, the first Greeks known to do so. The Persian center pushes through, but both Athenian wings rout their opponents and then wheel inward to encircle the advancing Persian center. The Persians are driven back to their ships; 6,400 Persians fall against 192 Athenians.

1027.modern-en: News of the defeat at Marathon reaches Darius and intensifies his determination to punish Athens. He spends three years in preparation — raising troops, ships, and supplies from across the empire — before a revolt in Egypt forces him to postpone the campaign. He dies before he can launch it, having never managed to avenge the humiliation on the plain of Marathon.

epithet.en: Persian Great King, leader of the invasion of Greece
epithet.da: Persisk Storkonge, leder af invasionen af Grækenland

1027.modern-en: Xerxes inherits his father Darius's unfinished war against Athens. Initially reluctant to campaign against Greece, he is persuaded by Mardonius and by dreams that seem to punish him whenever he resolves not to go. After putting down the Egyptian revolt, he spends four years preparing the largest invasion force ever assembled — bridging the Hellespont, digging a canal through the Athos peninsula, stockpiling supplies along the route.

1034.modern-en: Xerxes addresses the Persian nobles in council, laying out his case for the invasion of Greece. He argues that conquest is the inherited Persian way of life, that the gods have approved the campaign through his dreams, and that Greece is the logical next step after a continuous chain of conquests. His uncle Artabanus alone counsels restraint, warning that the sea and the land itself are the true enemies — larger forces mean greater vulnerability.

1044.modern-en: Artabanus, persuaded by Xerxes to sleep in the king's bed and test the dream himself, is visited by the same threatening vision and is almost blinded by it. He recants his opposition and tells Xerxes the gods are clearly driving this expedition forward. The episode suggests that divine compulsion, not rational calculation, is carrying Persia toward Greece — and possibly toward disaster.

1070.modern-en: Standing at the Hellespont, watching his vast army cross, Xerxes weeps. His uncle Artabanus asks why. Xerxes says: he was struck by pity for the brevity of human life — in a hundred years, not one of this great multitude will still be living. The moment of pathos at the peak of his power anticipates the unraveling to come.

1080.modern-en: Xerxes crosses the Hellespont into Europe — a passage that takes seven days and nights of continuous movement. A local man is said to have asked aloud why Zeus had taken the form of a Persian man and the name Xerxes, when he could simply have destroyed Greece himself without the trouble of leading an army. The scale of the crossing impresses and terrifies every observer.

1230.modern-en: Xerxes sends a scout to observe the Spartans at Thermopylae and is told they are exercising and combing their long hair — the Spartan custom before a battle they do not expect to survive. Demaratus, the exiled Spartan king at his court, tells Xerxes that these men are the finest fighters in Greece and will die rather than retreat. Xerxes finds this incredible and waits four days, expecting them to flee.

1244.modern-en: After four days of watching and two days of frontal assault that achieve nothing, Xerxes learns of the mountain path that will allow him to encircle Leonidas's force. He sends his Immortals around by night. The Greeks at the pass, warned by deserters and the soothsayer's sacrifices, prepare to make their last stand. Xerxes watches the final battle from a throne on the hillside.

1246.modern-en: The body of Leonidas becomes the center of fierce fighting after the final assault. The Greeks hold their own until the Persians who have gone around the mountain close in from behind. Even then, the remaining Spartans and Thespians withdraw to a hillock and fight to the last, using only their hands and teeth when their weapons are broken. Xerxes, in rage, has Leonidas's head cut off and fixed on a stake — an act Herodotus notes as very unlike Persian custom toward brave enemies.

1317.modern-en: At Salamis, the allied Greek commanders are on the verge of abandoning the island and retreating to the Isthmus. Themistocles, persuaded by the Athenian Mnesiphilus that a dispersed fleet will never fight together again, rushes to Eurybiades and argues passionately for staying. The debate among the allies is heated; Themistocles threatens to sail to Italy if the fleet withdraws, taking Athens's entire navy with him.

1343.modern-en: Before the Battle of Salamis, Themistocles addresses the Greek sailors, urging them to focus on what is better in their nature rather than what is worse — to be the men who liberated Greece rather than those who gave it up. The Greeks go into battle energized. Xerxes watches from a golden throne on a hilltop above the bay, expecting to see his fleet destroy the Greeks; instead he watches the Persian fleet collapse in the narrow channel.

1360.modern-en: After the defeat at Salamis, Xerxes consults his advisors about next steps. Mardonius proposes staying in Greece and continuing the campaign under his own command, volunteering to take responsibility for the outcome. Artemisia, the queen of Halicarnassus who is one of Xerxes's naval commanders, privately advises him to return to Persia and let Mardonius try — the empire's survival matters more than one campaign.

epithet.en: Spartan king who died defending the pass at Thermopylae
epithet.da: Spartansk konge der døde forsvarende passet ved Thermopylai

1160.modern-en: As Xerxes's invasion approaches, most Greek states either submit or stay neutral. The Greeks who resist send an advance force to hold the pass at Thermopylae — a narrow coastal gap where a small force can neutralize a large one. Leonidas commands the Spartans there. The position is both strategically sound and symbolically important: the Greeks are choosing to fight rather than yield.

1230.modern-en: Xerxes's scout observes the Spartans at Thermopylae and reports back that they are combing their long hair before the battle — the Spartan pre-battle custom that signals readiness to die. Demaratus, the exiled Spartan at Xerxes's court, explains what this means: these men obey the law, and the law commands them not to retreat. Leonidas and his men already know they are likely to die and are preparing themselves calmly.

1240.modern-en: As dawn approaches on the last day, the Greeks at Thermopylae receive news from three directions that the Persians have gone around them by the mountain path — from the soothsayer's sacrifices, from deserters, and from dawn watchmen. The allied contingents are dismissed by Leonidas; most obey. Only the Thespians choose to remain voluntarily; the Thebans are kept as unwilling hostages.

1242.modern-en: Herodotus reports that Leonidas may have been fulfilling a Delphic oracle that said either Sparta must fall or its king must die. He tried to send away even the soothsayer Megistias, who refused to leave. The evidence Herodotus finds most convincing is that Leonidas sent other allies away — yet kept only Spartans and those who chose to stay — suggesting he knew what was coming and acted to preserve the larger Greek force.

1243.modern-en: Only the Thespians and Thebans remain with the three hundred Spartans. The Thespians refuse to leave because they will not abandon their allies; the Thebans are kept by force as suspected Persian sympathizers. Leonidas makes no speech; the time for words is past. The small force prepares to fight in the open ground beyond the wall, where they will have more room to die fighting.

1244.modern-en: Xerxes waits until mid-morning before sending in his Immortals — perhaps hoping the Greeks will still surrender. When the fighting begins, the Greeks advance into the wider part of the pass and inflict enormous casualties. Herodotus notes that the Persians were driven forward by whips; they fell in the sea; they were trampled by their own men. The Persian losses far exceed anything the Greeks suffered.

1245.modern-en: Leonidas falls in the fighting, having proved himself, in Herodotus's judgment, a very good man. Two brothers of Xerxes also fall fighting over the body of Leonidas. The Greeks — knowing that the encircling force is coming — withdraw to a small hillock and fight their final stand there, using broken spear shafts and then swords and finally bare hands and teeth. They are overwhelmed only when the Persians shoot them down from all sides with arrows.

1246.modern-en: After the last Greek falls, Xerxes has Leonidas's head cut off and his body crucified — a treatment he normally reserves for Persian traitors, not for brave foreign enemies. Herodotus notes that this punishment was later administered to a Greek general who had surrendered rather than fight, suggesting Xerxes recognized, in his fury, that Leonidas's courage was something to be feared even in death.

epithet.en: Athenian strategist, architect of the Greek naval victory at Salamis
epithet.da: Atheniensisk strateg, arkitekt bag den græske sejr ved Salamis

1165.modern-en: Themistocles emerges as a new force among the Athenians when the Delphic oracle, warning of Persian attack, tells them to trust in their 'wooden walls.' Most interpreters say this means Athens's actual wooden wall on the Acropolis; Themistocles argues it means the navy. He persuades the Athenians to interpret the oracle as a command to build ships and fight at sea. His ability to read ambiguous signs where others see only one meaning is his defining characteristic.

1264.modern-en: At Artemisium, the Greek fleet is on the verge of retreating at the sight of the Persian armada. Themistocles, bribed by the Euboeans who need the fleet to stay and protect their coast, passes the money on to Eurybiades and to the Corinthian commander as private gifts to encourage them to remain. He keeps a share for himself, trusting his own judgment about where the fleet must fight.

1282.modern-en: Themistocles sails to the water sources used by the Persian fleet at Artemisium and carves messages into the stones asking the Ionian Greeks — serving in Xerxes's fleet under compulsion — to either join the Greek side or at least fight badly in the coming battle. The inscriptions serve two purposes: if the Ionians read them and defect, the Greek position improves; if Xerxes's commanders read them, they will suspect the Ionians of disloyalty anyway.

1317.modern-en: When the Greek commanders vote to withdraw from Salamis to the Isthmus, Themistocles is persuaded by the Athenian Mnesiphilus that a dispersed fleet will never reunite. He rushes to Eurybiades's ship and reverses the vote by sheer force of argument — threatening that Athens will sail its entire fleet to Italy if the allied commanders abandon Salamis. He understands that geography at Salamis favors the smaller Greek force.

1318.modern-en: Themistocles argues at the war council for staying at Salamis: in narrow water, Greek seamanship counts for more and the larger Persian fleet cannot bring its numbers to bear. The Corinthian Adeimantos tries to silence him by saying a man with no city has no vote; Themistocles replies that Athens has two hundred ships and a city wherever it goes. He wins the argument with a direct threat: abandon us and we sail for Italy.

1319.modern-en: To force the battle at Salamis and prevent any further retreat, Themistocles secretly sends his slave Sicinnus to the Persian commanders with false information: the Greeks are planning to escape by night, he says — if the Persians move now they can trap them all in the channel. The Persians believe it and blockade the strait overnight, cutting off the escape route that some Greek commanders still hoped to use.

1339.modern-en: At midnight before the battle, Aristides — Themistocles's old political enemy, just returned from ostracism — rows across to Salamis and reports that the Persian fleet has already encircled the island. He calls Themistocles out of the war council and tells him privately. Themistocles immediately shares the news with the other commanders, presenting it as confirmation of everything he had argued. Political rivalry gives way to necessity.

1343.modern-en: On the morning of the battle, Themistocles delivers a speech before the whole fleet, contrasting the better and worse in human nature and urging the sailors to choose the better. The Greeks fight with tremendous energy and disorder the Persian fleet in the narrow channel. Xerxes watches from his hilltop throne as his fleet is destroyed. The wooden walls have held.

1383.modern-en: After Salamis, Themistocles is voted the most admired man in Greece when all the commanders gather at the Isthmus to award prizes. Each man puts his own name first for valor and second for Themistocles — so Themistocles effectively wins the second-place vote of the entire assembly. Despite receiving no official honor from the allies, who cannot agree to give him the first prize, he is celebrated throughout Greece as the man who saved it.
